Question: Why did Winston Churchill during WW2 wear a military uniform when in fact he was Prime Minister? Montgomery was the leader of the Army.
Old_Answer: Churchill had served in the British Army in India and elsewhere at the end of the 19th century, and in France during WW1. It was also common for the British Army to appoint ‘Honorary Colonels’ to its regiments. Churchill was honorary colonel of several regiments. The RAF adopted the same practice of appointing honorary positions. In 1939 Churchill was appointed Hon. Air Commodore, No. 615 (County of Surrey) Squadron, Royal Auxiliary Air Force. The squadron was based at Kenley, only about ten miles from Chartwell and therefore easy for Churchill to visit. By 1940 it was operating Hurricanes and Spitfires. It was this uniform that Churchill frequently wore during the Second World War. On 1 April 1943, the twenty-fifth anniversary of the creation of the RAF, the Air Council with the King’s approval awarded honorary wings (the flying badge of the Royal Air Force) to the Prime Minister. Earlier in life Churchill had taken flying lessons, but at the insistence of his wife had given them up on safety grounds before achieving his ‘wings’. On January 12 1943, Churchill flew to Casablanca for a conference with Roosevelt, Marshall, Montgomery, Eisenhower and other leaders, including General “Pug” Ismay, Secretary of the Imperial Defence Chiefs of Staff Committee. For security purposes Churchill on arrival in Casablanca wore his air commodore uniform and was designated “Air Commodore Frankland”. Ismay was heard to mutter “Any fool can see that that is an Air Commodore disguised as a Prime Minister”.

Question: Why did the British people turn on Winston Churchill after the war when he ran for prime minister?
Old_Answer: I asked my father this same question about why Labour had been preferred to tthe Conservatives in 1945. My father had served in the RAF during the war - as a navigator - taking personnel and supplies into France to assist the Resistance. He said that he had voted Labour in the 1945 election. He cited four reasons for his vote: I think it is instructive to read the Conservative Party manifesto for the 1945 election. It is available at 1945 Conservative Party Manifesto. This document has every sign of being written by Winston Churchill. On demobilisation it says: “The broad and properly considered lines of the demobilisation proposals, based on age and length of service, which Mr. Bevin has elaborated with much wisdom, will be adhered to, and releases will be made as quickly as the condition of the tormented world permits.” By contrast the Labour Party manifesto (available at 1945 Labour Party Manifesto -) is silent on demobilisation. On Health the Conservative manifesto says: “The health services of the country will be made available to all citizens. Everyone will contribute to the cost, and no one will be denied the attention, the treatment or the appliances he requires because he cannot afford them. We propose to create a comprehensive health service covering the whole range of medical treatment from the general practitioner to the specialist, and from the hospital to convalescence and rehabilitation; and to introduce legislation for this purpose in the new Parliament.” On employment, the Conservative manifesto says: “In the White Paper presented to Parliament by the late administration are sound plans for avoiding the disastrous slumps and booms from which we used to suffer, but which all are united in being determined to avoid in the future. The Government accepts as one of its primary aims and responsibilities the maintenance of a high and stable level of employment.” On India the Conservative manifesto says: “The prowess of the Indian Army must not be overlooked in the framing of plans for granting India a fuller opportunity to achieve Dominion Status We should remember those friends who stood by us in our hour of peril, and should be ever mindful of our obligations towards minorities and the Indian States.” Looking back in hindsight, I think a Churchill government would actually have done a better job on all these items. I don’t think Churchill would have sent Mountbatten to India and I think he would have made a much greater effort to reconcile the parties and avoid the horrific bloodshed there. Clearly the substantive proposals put forward by the parties were not the reason for Labour’s victory in 1945. The Labour party quite simply did a much better job of putting their message across to the people - especially those in the armed services. Churchill had wanted to delay the election until after the defeat of Japan. He was distracted by the Potsdam conference and the strident demands of the Soviet Union. He took his re-election for granted and didn’t make the necessary effort required to achieve it. Churchill did win the election in 1951, which ushered in a long period of Conservative power. I think there were two major reasons for Conservative success in 1951: One of my earliest memories is walking around the neighbourhood of my grandmother’s home in South London. About every tenth house had been destroyed by bombs, and most of the lots still stayed there untouched with weeds growing over the ruins. Another memory is going to the shops with my aunt and seeing that she had to hand over ration tickets along with cash to buy basic foodstuffs.
